(CNN) — A Colorado prosecutor on Friday asked a judge to dismiss the first-degree murder charge against Tim Masters, who spent nine years in prison before new DNA evidence indicated that someone else may have committed the crime.

Tim Masters, center, walked out of a Fort Collins, Colorado, courthouse Tuesday with his attorney, David Wymore.

Court papers filed by District Attorney Larry Abrahamson cited “newly discovered” evidence, while carefully emphasizing that the evidence did not clear Masters.

“While the newly discovered DNA evidence does not exonerate Timothy Masters, it clearly warrants a complete re-examination of all the evidence related to the murder of Peggy Hettrick,” the court papers state.

The motion seeks dismissal of the charges “in the interest of justice.” It notes that the DNA testing used to uncover the new evidence was not available when Masters was investigated and tried.

On Tuesday, a judge vacated Masters’ 1999 murder conviction, and he was released—also “in the interest of justice.”

Although the motion indicates that Abrahamson is dropping the case against Masters, he did not rule out future prosecution.

In a statement, the prosecutor cautioned: “Contrary to news reports, the DNA testing results only suggest that there may be others, along with Timothy Masters, who should be investigated. These test results do not provide us with enough information to completely exonerate anyone.”

Abrahamson said he has asked Colorado Attorney General John Suthers to appoint a special prosecutor to continue the investigation into Hettrick’s killing. The attorney general will announce his decision early next week, Abrahamson said.

Masters, 36, has been under investigation in connection with Hettrick’s murder since he was 15. He has consistently maintained that he had nothing to do with her death, and no physical evidence directly ties him to the crime.

A jury convicted Masters 12 years after Hettrick’s stabbed and sexually mutilated body was discovered in a field near his trailer. Among the evidence jurors considered were a collection of knives found in Masters’ bedroom, gruesome sketches, and testimony from a prosecution expert who said Masters fit the psychological profile of a killer.

Masters’ defense team said he was framed and that police and prosecutors withheld evidence that could have raised doubt about his guilt.

The significance of Friday’s motion to dismiss is largely procedural, but Abrahamson indicated earlier this week that it might be unnecessary to try Masters again.

“In light of newly discovered evidence revealed to me on Friday,” Abrahamson said in a statement a week ago, “I will be moving as expeditiously as possible to make the determination of whether all charges against Timothy Masters will be dismissed.”

Abrahamson also has pledged to review all “contested convictions” in which advances in DNA testing may prove useful. He said he wanted to examine the legal discovery process and had met with the Fort Collins police chief and his officers “to discuss the critical flow of information with assurance that all information is available to our office and the defense.”

Special prosecutor Don Quick filed a motion earlier this month citing four instances in which police and prosecutors should have turned over evidence to Masters’ original defense team.

Among them was a police interview with a plastic surgeon who said it was improbable that a teenager could have made the meticulous cuts necessary to remove Hettrick’s body parts. According to Quick’s motion, police also failed to disclose that a renowned FBI profiler had warned investigators that Masters’ tendency to doodle gruesome horror scenes did not connect him to the crime.

Investigations into how police and prosecutors handled the case are continuing.

# Dismissal Motion Revives Questions Over Evidence in Tim Masters Wrongful Conviction Case

**FORT COLLINS, Colorado** — A legal fight tied to one of Colorado’s most notorious wrongful conviction cases has again placed scrutiny on the investigation of the 1987 killing of Peggy Hettrick, the prosecution of former suspect and exoneree Tim Masters, and long-running questions about whether key evidence was withheld from the defense.

Masters, who spent nearly a decade in prison after being convicted of Hettrick’s murder, has maintained that police and prosecutors built a case around speculation, ignored evidence pointing away from him, and failed to disclose information that could have helped his defense. His conviction was vacated in 2008 after DNA testing implicated another man and undermined the theory used to convict him.

At the center of the latest legal dispute is a dismissal motion filed by defendants in civil litigation stemming from Masters’ wrongful conviction claims. The motion asks the court to throw out some or all of the claims, arguing that the allegations do not meet the legal threshold for liability or that certain defendants are protected by legal immunity. Masters’ side has argued that the case involves serious constitutional violations, including the alleged suppression of favorable evidence and misconduct during the investigation and prosecution.

## A Killing That Haunted Fort Collins

Peggy Hettrick, 37, was found dead in a field in Fort Collins in February 1987. Her killing shocked the community and quickly became one of the city’s most closely watched homicide investigations.

Masters was 15 years old at the time and lived near the area where Hettrick’s body was found. He came under police attention partly because of his proximity to the crime scene and because investigators collected drawings and writings from him that they interpreted as violent or suspicious.

For years, however, the case remained unsolved. Masters denied involvement, and physical evidence did not directly connect him to the killing. Despite that, investigators continued to focus on him.

More than a decade later, prosecutors charged Masters with murder. In 1999, he was convicted and sentenced to life in prison without parole.

## The Theory Used at Trial

At trial, prosecutors relied heavily on circumstantial evidence and expert testimony about Masters’ drawings, writings and alleged psychological profile. The state argued that his artwork and statements reflected a fascination with violence and linked him to the mutilation of Hettrick’s body.

The prosecution’s case did not include eyewitness testimony placing Masters at the scene during the killing. Nor did it include physical evidence tying him to Hettrick’s body. Instead, the case depended on a narrative that Masters had long harbored violent fantasies and that the details in his drawings showed knowledge of the crime.

Masters’ attorneys later argued that this theory was deeply flawed and that the defense had not been given access to important information that could have challenged the state’s case.

## DNA Testing Changes the Case

Masters’ conviction began to unravel after post-conviction review and DNA testing raised serious doubts about his guilt.

In 2008, Masters was released from prison after DNA evidence found on Hettrick’s clothing was linked not to him, but to another man. That evidence helped lead prosecutors to ask that his conviction be vacated. Masters was later formally exonerated.

The DNA development was a turning point, but it did not answer all questions about how the case against him was built — or why evidence that may have assisted his defense was not fully disclosed before trial.

## Claims of Withheld Evidence

A central issue in Masters’ wrongful conviction claims is whether investigators and prosecutors failed to turn over material evidence favorable to the defense, as required under the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in *Brady v. Maryland*.

Under *Brady*, prosecutors must disclose evidence that is favorable to the accused and material to guilt or punishment. That obligation can include impeachment evidence, alternative-suspect information, forensic inconsistencies and investigative notes that weaken the state’s theory.

Masters’ legal team has alleged that authorities withheld or failed to properly disclose evidence that would have helped his defense, including information about alternative suspects, investigative leads and material that challenged the state’s interpretation of his drawings and writings.

Questions have also been raised about whether defense attorneys at trial were given a complete picture of investigative doubts, competing theories and evidence pointing away from Masters. His supporters have argued that if jurors had heard the full story, the prosecution’s circumstantial case would have looked far weaker.

## The Dismissal Motion

The dismissal motion asks the court to end the case before it proceeds further, or to narrow the claims and defendants. Such motions are common in civil-rights litigation, especially in wrongful conviction cases, where defendants often include prosecutors, police officers, municipalities or counties.

The defendants’ arguments typically focus on several legal defenses:

- **Absolute prosecutorial immunity:** Prosecutors are often shielded from civil liability for actions closely tied to their role as advocates in court, such as presenting evidence or deciding how to prosecute a case.  
- **Qualified immunity:** Police officers and other officials may be protected unless they violated clearly established constitutional rights.  
- **Failure to state a claim:** Defendants may argue that even if the alleged facts are accepted as true, they do not amount to a legally valid claim.  
- **Causation:** Defendants may contend that alleged misconduct did not directly cause the conviction.  
- **Municipal liability limits:** Claims against counties or cities must show that a policy, custom or failure to train caused the constitutional violation.

Masters’ side has argued that the case is not merely about trial strategy or good-faith investigative mistakes, but about alleged misconduct that deprived him of a fair trial and caused years of wrongful imprisonment.

## Why the Motion Matters

The court’s handling of the dismissal motion could determine how much of Masters’ case proceeds to discovery or trial.

If the motion is granted in full, Masters’ claims could be dismissed without a full airing of evidence in civil court. If it is denied, the case could move forward, potentially allowing depositions, document production and deeper examination of what investigators and prosecutors knew at various stages of the Hettrick investigation.

If granted in part, some defendants or claims could be removed while others remain.

Wrongful conviction cases often hinge on this stage because courts must balance two competing interests: allowing people who were allegedly framed or denied a fair trial to seek accountability, while also protecting public officials from lawsuits over decisions made during criminal investigations and prosecutions.

## Broader Questions About Accountability

Masters’ case has become a major example in debates over wrongful convictions, forensic uncertainty and prosecutorial disclosure obligations.

His conviction showed how a case built largely on behavioral interpretation, artwork and circumstantial theory can become persuasive to a jury even without direct physical evidence. His exoneration, years later, highlighted the importance of DNA testing and post-conviction review.

But the lingering issue is whether the justice system merely made a mistake — or whether officials failed to disclose evidence that could have prevented the conviction.

For Masters and his supporters, the answer is clear: they say the case represents a breakdown in constitutional protections and investigative fairness. For defendants seeking dismissal, the civil claims must meet strict legal standards, and some actions may be shielded by immunity even if the conviction was later vacated.

## The Hettrick Case Remains a Painful Chapter

The dismissal fight also underscores that Peggy Hettrick’s murder remains the tragedy at the heart of the case. Her death devastated those who knew her and left Fort Collins searching for answers for decades.

Masters’ exoneration shifted attention away from him and toward questions about other possible suspects and the handling of the original investigation. But the legal record surrounding the case continues to focus on whether police and prosecutors became too fixated on a teenage neighbor while failing to fully pursue or disclose evidence that complicated their theory.

## What Comes Next

The court must decide whether Masters’ wrongful conviction claims can continue and, if so, against whom. That decision could shape the next phase of one of Colorado’s most consequential criminal justice cases.

For Masters, the litigation is about accountability for years lost behind bars. For the defendants, the dismissal motion is an effort to end claims they argue are legally insufficient or barred by immunity. For the public, the case raises enduring questions about evidence disclosure, tunnel vision and the safeguards meant to prevent wrongful convictions.

Whatever the court decides, the Tim Masters case remains a stark reminder that a murder investigation can produce two separate quests for justice: one for the victim, and one for the person wrongfully convicted of the crime.

**Man convicted in 1987 murder walks out of Fort Collins courthouse after prosecutor seeks dismissal**

**FORT COLLINS, Colorado (CNN)** — Tim Masters, who spent years in prison for a murder he has long insisted he did not commit, walked out of a Fort Collins courthouse Tuesday after prosecutors asked a judge to dismiss the charges against him in the 1987 killing of Peggy Hettrick.

Masters, a former Navy mechanic, had been convicted in 1999 in Hettrick’s death and sentenced to life in prison. His attorneys argued that key evidence was withheld from the defense and that advances in DNA testing cast serious doubt on the case that sent him to prison.

The request to dismiss the charges marks a dramatic turn in one of Colorado’s most closely watched murder cases. Prosecutors said the available evidence no longer supported continuing the case against Masters.

Outside the courthouse, Masters appeared relieved but restrained, saying he wanted time to process what had happened after years of fighting to clear his name.

Hettrick, 37, was found stabbed and mutilated in a field in Fort Collins in February 1987. Masters, who was 15 at the time and lived nearby, became a focus of investigators early in the case. He was not charged until more than a decade later.

The conviction drew renewed scrutiny after defense attorneys uncovered information they said should have been turned over before trial, including evidence that pointed to other possible suspects. DNA testing also became a central issue in the push to overturn the conviction.

A judge previously ordered Masters released from prison while the case was re-examined. The prosecutor’s request to dismiss the charges goes further, effectively ending the murder case against him if approved by the court.

Meanwhile, questions remain about how the original investigation and prosecution were handled. Authorities have launched an inquiry into whether police and prosecutors failed to disclose evidence or otherwise mishandled the Hettrick case.

That investigation is expected to review decisions made by Fort Collins police and members of the prosecution team over the years, including what evidence was collected, how it was interpreted and whether defense attorneys were given access to all material that could have helped Masters at trial.

Hettrick’s murder remains under review, and officials have not announced new charges against anyone else.

For Masters, the courthouse exit was a long-awaited moment. But for Hettrick’s family — and for a community that has followed the case for more than two decades — the dismissal raises new questions about who killed her and whether the justice system failed both the victim and the man convicted of her murder.
